title: No. 82 — The Judiciary Continued. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The creation of a new government, however much care or wisdom marks the work, cannot fail to raise questions of intricacy and nicety. These may be expected to arise in a special way from establishing a constitution founded on the total or partial incorporation of a number of distinct sovereignties. Only time can mature and perfect so compound a system, settle the meaning of all its parts, and adjust them to one another in a harmonious and consistent WHOLE.

Such questions have accordingly arisen on the plan proposed by the Convention, particularly concerning the judiciary department. The principal ones concern the position of the State courts with respect to those causes that are to be submitted to federal jurisdiction. Is this jurisdiction to be exclusive, or are those courts to have a concurrent jurisdiction? If the latter, what relation will they have to the national courts? These are inquiries we hear from men of sense, and they certainly deserve attention.

The principles established in an earlier paper(1) teach us that the States will keep all pre-existing authorities that are not exclusively delegated to the federal head, and that exclusive delegation can exist only in one of three cases. The first is where an exclusive authority is granted to the Union in express terms. The second is where a particular authority is granted to the Union and the exercise of a like authority is forbidden to the States. The third is where an authority is granted to the Union with which a similar authority in the States would be utterly incompatible. These principles may not apply with the same force to the judiciary as to the legislative power. Still, I am inclined to think they are, in the main, just with respect to the former as well as the latter. With this in mind, I shall lay it down as a rule that the State courts will keep the jurisdiction they now have, unless it appears to be taken away in one of the ways I have listed.

The only thing in the proposed Constitution that has the appearance of confining causes of federal jurisdiction to the federal courts is this passage: "THE JUDICIAL POWER of the United States shall be vested in one Supreme Court, and in such inferior courts as the Congress shall from time to time ordain and establish." This might be construed to mean that the supreme and subordinate courts of the Union alone should have the power of deciding those causes to which their authority is to extend. Or it might simply denote that the organs of the national judiciary should be one Supreme Court and as many subordinate courts as Congress should think proper to appoint. In other words, the United States would exercise the judicial power with which they are to be invested through one supreme court and a certain number of inferior ones, to be instituted by them. The first construction excludes the concurrent jurisdiction of the State courts; the last admits it. And since the first would amount to a transfer of State power by implication, the last appears to me the most natural and the most defensible construction.

But this doctrine of concurrent jurisdiction clearly applies only to those kinds of causes of which the State courts have previous jurisdiction. It is not equally evident in relation to cases that may grow out of, and be peculiar to, the Constitution to be established; for denying the State courts jurisdiction in such cases can hardly be considered a curtailment of a pre-existing authority. I do not mean to contend, therefore, that the United States, in legislating on the objects entrusted to their direction, may not commit the decision of causes arising under a particular regulation solely to the federal courts, if such a measure should be thought expedient. But I hold that the State courts will lose no part of their original jurisdiction, except as it may relate to an appeal; and I am even of the opinion that in every case in which they are not expressly excluded by future acts of the national legislature, they will of course take jurisdiction of the causes to which those acts may give birth. I infer this from the nature of judicial power and from the general character of the system. The judicial power of every government looks beyond its own local or municipal laws, and in civil cases takes hold of all subjects of litigation between parties within its jurisdiction, though the causes of dispute relate to the laws of the most distant part of the globe. Those of Japan, no less than those of New York, may furnish matters of legal discussion to our courts. When in addition we consider the State governments and the national government as they truly are, as kindred systems and as parts of ONE WHOLE, the inference seems conclusive that the State courts would have a concurrent jurisdiction in all cases arising under the laws of the Union, where it was not expressly prohibited.

Here another question arises: what relation would exist between the national and State courts in these instances of concurrent jurisdiction? I answer that an appeal would certainly lie from the latter to the Supreme Court of the United States. The Constitution in direct terms gives the Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction in all the listed cases of federal jurisdiction in which it is not to have original jurisdiction, without a single expression to confine this to the inferior federal courts. Only the objects of appeal are contemplated, not the courts from which the appeal is to be made. From this circumstance, and from the reason of the thing, the provision ought to be construed to extend to the State courts. Either this must be the case, or the local courts must be excluded from concurrent jurisdiction in matters of national concern; otherwise the judicial authority of the Union may be evaded at the pleasure of every plaintiff or prosecutor. Neither of these consequences ought to be accepted without evident necessity. The latter would be entirely inadmissible, as it would defeat some of the most important and avowed purposes of the proposed government and would seriously hamper its measures. Nor do I see any foundation for such a supposition. As I have already remarked, the national and State systems are to be regarded as ONE WHOLE. The courts of the latter will naturally be auxiliaries in executing the laws of the Union, and an appeal from them will as naturally lie to the court that is destined to unite and bring into line the principles of national justice and the rules of national decisions. The evident aim of the plan of the Convention is that all the causes of the specified classes shall, for weighty public reasons, receive their original or final determination in the courts of the Union. To confine the general expressions giving appellate jurisdiction to the Supreme Court to appeals from the subordinate federal courts, instead of allowing them to extend to the State courts, would be to narrow the breadth of the terms and defeat their intent, contrary to every sound rule of interpretation.

But could an appeal lie from the State courts to the subordinate federal courts? This is another question that has been raised, and a harder one than the last. The following considerations favor the affirmative. First, the plan of the Convention authorizes the national legislature "to constitute tribunals inferior to the Supreme Court."(2) Next, it declares that "the JUDICIAL POWER of the United States shall be vested in one Supreme Court, and in such inferior courts as Congress shall ordain and establish"; and it then lists the cases to which this judicial power shall extend. It afterwards divides the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court into original and appellate, but defines nothing for the subordinate courts. The only outlines drawn for them are that they shall be "inferior to the Supreme Court" and that they shall not go beyond the specified limits of the federal judiciary. Whether their authority is to be original or appellate, or both, is not stated. All of this seems to be left to the discretion of the legislature. That being so, I see at present no obstacle to establishing an appeal from the State courts to the subordinate national courts, and many advantages of having that power can be imagined. It would lessen the motive to multiply federal courts and would allow arrangements to narrow the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. The State courts could then be left with fuller charge of federal causes; and appeals, in most cases where they are thought proper, instead of going to the Supreme Court, could lie from the State courts to district courts of the Union.
